subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Repeated Games and Reputation
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Repeated Games and Reputation.

hook.text: A seller cheats once and earns $100. Word spreads. No one buys from them again.

buildup.text: Repeated games change strategy. When you interact again, today's defection invites tomorrow's punishment.

discovery.text: Axelrod's tournaments proved Tit for Tat wins: cooperate first, then mirror the other's last move.

twist.text: If the game has a known endpoint, cooperation unravels from the end. Knowing the last round, both defect.

climax.text: Reputation is the mechanism. In repeated interactions, your track record is your strategy.

punchline.text: Reputation takes years to build and seconds to lose.

quiz.question: What strategy won Axelrod's repeated game tournaments?
options: Always defect to maximize individual gain
Tit for Tat: cooperate first, then mirror the other's last move

details.summary: In repeated games, players build reputations by establishing consistent behavioral patterns, and the shadow of future interaction sustains cooperation that would be impossible in a one-shot encounter.
details.whyItMatters: Most real-world strategic interactions are repeated. The ability to build reputation and threat of future retaliation transforms incentives, making cooperation self-enforcing in relationships, business, and international relations.
takeaways: Repeated interaction enables cooperation through future consequences
Reputation acts as a commitment device that constrains future behavior
End-game effects cause cooperation to unravel in finitely repeated games

faq.question: Why does cooperation collapse near the end of repeated games?
faq.answer: In the last round, there is no future to incentivize cooperation, so players defect. Knowing this, they defect in the second-to-last round too. This backward unraveling theoretically destroys cooperation, though humans often cooperate longer.

faq.question: How does reputation building work strategically?
faq.answer: A player who consistently cooperates early builds a reputation that encourages others to cooperate with them. This reputation is a strategic asset that pays off over many interactions, making initial costly cooperation a worthwhile investment.
